card: UN Headquarters, New York. 23 October to 20 November · 8 decisions. With the Security Council deadlocked by the veto, you stand between two great powers with nothing but a sheet of paper.
intro: You are U Thant, 53, a Burmese diplomat and acting secretary-general of the United Nations. Since Secretary-General Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash over the Congo in September 1961, you have led the Secretariat for thirteen months as “acting” secretary-general; your election to a full term still awaits a vote of the General Assembly. You have no army and no votes. You have only the right Article 99 of the Charter gives you, to “bring to the attention of the Security Council” any threat to peace, and the trust that brings member delegates to your door. Beside you are Ralph Bunche, under-secretary for special political affairs; Omar Loutfi, the Egyptian under-secretary; Narasimhan, your chef de cabinet; and your military adviser, Brigadier Rikhye. In the lobby outside the chamber, the delegates of some fifty non-aligned states from Asia, Africa and the Arab world have gathered. In the chamber, Stevenson of the United States, Zorin of the Soviet Union (president of the Security Council for October) and García-Incháustegui of Cuba each hold a different draft resolution. On your dashboard, “Ally Trust” is the trust of the Security Council members, and “Home Support” is the support of the Secretariat and the non-aligned bloc. What you can do is write letters, meet people and get on airplanes. With those three things you must see this crisis through.

UT-01.place: UN Headquarters, New York: the Secretary-General’s anteroom beside the Security Council chamber
UT-01.title: Three Requests for a Meeting

telegram.from: Adlai Stevenson, Permanent Representative of the United States of America
telegram.to: The President of the Security Council
telegram.subject: Request for an urgent meeting of the Security Council
telegram.text: I have the honor to request an urgent meeting of the Security Council to deal with the dangerous threat to the peace and security of the world caused by the secret establishment in Cuba by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics of launching bases and the installation of long-range ballistic missiles capable of carrying thermonuclear warheads to most of North and South America. / The United States has incontrovertible evidence that the Soviet Union has been installing in Cuba a whole series of facilities for launching offensive nuclear missiles and other offensive weapons, and installing the weapons themselves. / On 11 September the Soviet Government said in an official statement that the armaments and military equipment sent to Cuba were designed exclusively for defensive purposes.

UT-01.event: At 7 p.m. last night President Kennedy went on television to reveal the Soviet missile bases in Cuba and declare a naval quarantine. That same night the United States (S/5181) and Cuba (S/5183), and this morning the Soviet Union (S/5186), each asked for a meeting of the Security Council. The American draft resolution, S/5182, calls for the removal of the missiles under UN supervision as a provisional measure under Article 40 of the Charter; the Soviet draft, S/5187, calls for the blockade to be condemned. The president of the Security Council for October is the Soviet representative, Zorin. No one has yet told the Secretariat when the quarantine will start being enforced at sea.
UT-01.scene: The 1022nd meeting opens at 4 p.m. You are a Burmese who has led the Secretariat for thirteen months as “acting” secretary-general since Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash over the Congo, and in two months a vote will decide your full term. In the chamber Stevenson cites photographs of the missile bases, the Cuban ambassador, García-Incháustegui, calls the blockade an act of war, and Zorin, from the president’s chair, retorts that the United States has produced no evidence. None of the three resolutions can pass: the American one will meet a Soviet veto, and the Soviet one, if it ever comes to a vote, Western opposition. Bunche says that if the Secretary-General speaks on the first day, he will be read as taking sides. Loutfi reports that the Asian and African delegates are already looking for you outside the chamber. Article 99 of the Charter says only that the Secretary-General may bring to the attention of the Security Council a matter that threatens the peace; it grants no power beyond that.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary for special political affairs)
voices.text: Secretary-General, today you must listen. On a day when three countries have each asked for a meeting, if the Secretary-General speaks first, he will sound like a judge, not a mediator. Even Hammarskjöld waited on the first day of Suez.

voices.who: Omar Loutfi (under-secretary, former Egyptian ambassador)
voices.text: The Arab, African and Asian delegates are gathering in the lobby outside the chamber. They know the Council will be blocked by the veto, and they want the Secretary-General to move. Waiting tonight is fine. But if you wait tomorrow as well, someone else will take your place.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative, in the chamber)
voices.text: What the Soviet Union has brought into Cuba are not defensive weapons. The United States has the evidence, and the Council must order their removal under UN supervision, as Article 40 of the Charter provides.

choices.text: Say nothing in the chamber and follow the debate. In the evening, hear out the non-aligned delegates with Bunche and Loutfi
choices.why: Silence on the first day protects the Secretary-General’s neutrality
choices.after: The meeting ended at 8:20 p.m. You did not speak, and the next day’s papers reported that the Secretary-General had kept silent. That night, at a mission near UN Headquarters, delegates of about 50 countries met for nearly three hours and agreed to meet again in the morning.

choices.text: Open the meeting with a statement appealing to the three parties for restraint, and announce that you will begin direct consultations under Article 99 of the Charter
choices.why: The Secretary-General’s voice must come before a Council the veto will block
choices.after: The chamber heard the statement politely, but Zorin resented that the Secretary-General had said nothing about the illegality of the blockade, and Stevenson was disappointed that he had said nothing about the missiles. That night nearly 50 delegations met; knowing now that the Secretary-General was willing to act, they agreed to send people to him in the morning.

choices.text: After the meeting, call Stevenson and Zorin separately to your office and hear each side’s terms in private
choices.why: The real terms come out behind closed doors, not in an open chamber
choices.after: Stevenson came up at 10 p.m.; Zorin put it off until the next morning. Stevenson said that if the Soviet ships did not turn back, something would happen at sea on Wednesday morning. When he had gone, you sat up all night drafting a cable.

note.text: The president of the Security Council in October 1962 was the Soviet Union’s Zorin. Of the eleven members, seven could be counted on to back the American draft, but the Soviet veto meant neither draft could be adopted. On the 25th Rusk told ExComm that a Council vote would go about 7 to 2.

map.caption: UN Headquarters stands on the East River in Manhattan, New York. The Security Council met on 23 October.

UT-01.unknown: At that hour Washington had set the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) to take effect at 10 a.m. on 24 October, Washington time. Washington was also making its own count of the Security Council vote; on the 25th Rusk told ExComm it would be about 7 to 2.

UT-02.title: United Nations Day
UT-02.clock: 1 hour 30 minutes until the 1024th meeting of the Security Council (4 p.m.)

telegram.cls: Public (read out at the Security Council)
telegram.from: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.to: The President of the United States / the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR (through their permanent representatives)
telegram.subject: Urgent appeal on the present crisis
telegram.text: I have been asked by the Permanent Representatives of a large number of Member Governments of the United Nations to address an urgent appeal to you in the present critical situation. These representatives feel that in the interest of international peace and security, all concerned should refrain from any action which may aggravate the situation and bring with it the risk of war. / In their view it is important that time should be given to enable the parties concerned to get together with a view to resolving the present crisis peacefully and normalizing the situation in the Caribbean. This involves on the one hand the voluntary suspension of all arms shipments to Cuba, and also the voluntary suspension of the quarantine measures involving the searching of ships bound for Cuba. I believe that such voluntary suspension for a period of two to three weeks will greatly ease the situation and give time to the parties concerned to meet and discuss with a view to finding a peaceful solution of the problem. In this context, I shall gladly make myself available to all parties for whatever services I may be able to perform. / I urgently appeal to Your Excellency to give immediate consideration to this message. / I have sent an identical message to the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR [in the Moscow copy: to the President of the United States of America].

UT-02.event: At 10 a.m. the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) took effect. It is past midday, and no wire report has yet confirmed what the Soviet ships approaching the line are doing. Early in the morning Quaison-Sackey of Ghana, Rossides of Cyprus and Riad of the United Arab Republic came to you on behalf of about 50 delegations and asked you to appeal to the two leaders. Ghana and the UAR have tabled draft resolution S/5190, asking the Secretary-General to consult the parties at once. The Brazilian and Mexican delegates are talking of trading a halt to shipments for the withdrawal of American warships, leading later to a nuclear-free zone in Latin America.
UT-02.scene: Today is the seventeenth anniversary of the day the UN Charter came into force. You have decided to send Kennedy and Khrushchev, at 6 p.m., the identical cable you wrote overnight, and to read it out at the 4 p.m. meeting. At 2:30 Stevenson came up. He has read the cable and is disappointed that it says not one word about the missiles or the building of the bases; he asks you to hold it for 24 hours. You refused, but agreed to see him again at 5. The non-aligned delegates say that if the Secretary-General does not act today they will put their own resolution to a vote, and that resolution leans toward the Soviet side; the West will oppose it. Bunche says that unless the cable calls for a halt to construction inside Cuba, Washington will read the appeal as pro-Soviet. Loutfi says that if you mention the missiles, Cuba and the non-aligned will walk away. An hour and a half remains before the reading.

voices.who: Mahmoud Riad (United Arab Republic, 1024th meeting of the Security Council)
voices.text: Last night the representatives of some 50 Member States, fearful of an armed clash, desirous of a peaceful settlement and fully aware of the dangers inherent in the situation, met for almost three hours. They agreed that the situation was grave and that every effort must be made to save mankind from the disastrous consequences of a possible armed conflict. The same representatives met again this morning for the same purpose and chose the representatives of Ghana and Cyprus and myself to call on the Acting Secretary-General and convey to him their deep concern and anxiety.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative, 2:30 p.m.)
voices.text: Secretary-General, there are no missiles in this cable. No base construction either. Trade a halt to shipments for a halt to the quarantine, and the Soviets simply finish the work inside Cuba. Give us 24 hours. Washington needs time to prepare a reply.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary for special political affairs, after Stevenson has left)
voices.text: Washington will say this cable is vague about verification and says nothing about the missiles already in Cuba. They will also say they asked you to hold it and you refused. What they will call this appeal tonight, I cannot tell you.

choices.text: Send the non-aligned delegates’ appeal unchanged at 6 p.m., and add to your evening speech an appeal to halt construction of military facilities inside Cuba
choices.why: The same text to both leaders, and a separate word to Cuba, keeps you a mediator
choices.after: When Stevenson and Yost came back at 5, the cable had already gone. Stevenson asked you to put a halt to construction into your speech; you agreed to that, but said nothing about the missiles already there. At the evening meeting you read out the cable and appealed to Cuba, and on Aiken’s proposal the meeting was adjourned to 4 p.m. the next day. At 7:30 p.m. Zorin came to see you.

choices.text: Do as Stevenson asks: hold the cable for 24 hours and rewrite it to call for a halt to missile-base construction inside Cuba
choices.why: An appeal the United States cannot accept is no appeal at all
choices.after: The non-aligned delegates were furious. Riad said the Secretary-General was keeping to America’s timetable, and Ghana and the UAR demanded a vote on their resolution that night. The cable went out on the morning of the 25th, and that morning the Pentagon announced that the Soviet tanker Bucharest had reached the quarantine line overnight.

choices.text: Send no appeal and wait for a vote on S/5190, the Ghana–UAR resolution. The Secretary-General’s authority is what the Security Council gives him
choices.why: A secretary-general who acts without a Council mandate does not last
choices.after: At the evening meeting you had no cable to read. S/5190 never came to a vote, because the United States objected that “consultations among the parties” would cover up the missiles. That night no word came to the Secretary-General from either Moscow or Washington.

note.text: The record names the sponsors of the appeal only as “a large number of Member Governments.” The next day Quaison-Sackey said the representatives of Ghana, Cyprus and the UAR had called on the Secretary-General “on behalf of some 50 Member States.” On the 25th the New York Times ran the front-page headline “Thant Asks U.S. and Soviet for Two-Week Halt.” On the night of the 24th, on the telephone to Kennedy, Macmillan called the cable “a very dangerous message” (excerpt).

pressure.title: The Seventeenth UN Day
pressure.text: The authors of the appeal are not you but the non-aligned delegates working outside the chamber. Riad told you that delegates of some 50 countries had met for nearly three hours the night before and sent the representatives of Ghana, Cyprus and the UAR to the Secretary-General, and the first sentence of your cable, too, says that the permanent representatives of a large number of member governments asked for it. Stevenson, disappointed that it said not one word about the missiles or the building of the bases, asked for a 24-hour delay, and you refused. He is coming back up at 5. Whether Washington will read the appeal as siding with Moscow or as a way out, you cannot tell from what Stevenson says. An acting secretary-general facing a vote on his full term in two months is making his first public move in the name of the non-aligned, and whether that exposes the weakness of the office or becomes its strength depends on the answers the two capitals send tonight.

UT-02.unknown: At that hour the Soviet ships had already been ordered back from Moscow, but Washington had not yet confirmed it, and Havana had deployed 50 anti-aircraft batteries. At ExComm at 5 p.m. that day Rusk reported that “U Thant’s appeal will have only a vague reference to verification and nothing about the actual missiles in Cuba,” and that he had asked you to hold it up and you had refused. That night Kennedy said Khrushchev had to be given a way out, a way to stop his shipments without looking as though he had backed down completely, and your appeal became that way out. On the telephone to Kennedy that night, Macmillan called the cable “a very dangerous message.” Khrushchev’s letter calling the blockade “outright piracy” reached Kennedy at 9:24 p.m., Washington time.

UT-03.title: One Typewritten Page
UT-03.clock: 5 hours 30 minutes until the 1025th meeting of the Security Council (4 p.m.)

telegram.from: U.S. Permanent Representative Stevenson (delivered by hand)
telegram.subject: Elements for a message from the Secretary-General to Chairman Khrushchev
telegram.text: I. Expression of concern that, since Soviet ships are under instructions to challenge the quarantine, a confrontation at sea between Soviet ships and ships of the Western Hemisphere may occur which could lead to an escalation of violence. / II. Expression of concern that such a confrontation would destroy any possibility of the talks you have proposed as a prelude to a political settlement. / III. Expression of hope that Soviet ships will stay away from the interception area for a limited period, so that the modalities of an agreement can be discussed. / IV. Expression of your assurance that, on the basis that Soviet ships will not proceed toward Cuba, the United States will for the same period avoid direct confrontation with those ships in order to minimize the risk of any untoward incident.
telegram.sign: (handwritten in the margin) Handed to the Acting Secretary-General by Stevenson, 10:30 a.m., 25 October

UT-03.event: At 7:30 last night Zorin came to your office and called the appeal “a very bad proposal.” The blockade, he said, was wholly illegal, so the Secretary-General should take up its legality, and he must not put the lifting of the quarantine on the same footing as halting ships bound for Cuba. You replied that you were concerned not with legality but with averting a crisis. After midnight Stevenson woke you with a telephone call. Kennedy wanted the Secretary-General to appeal again, this time for the Soviet ships to stay outside the interception line for a few days, and you said you would do it in the morning.
UT-03.scene: Since the telephone call after midnight you have barely slept. The morning news says the tanker Bucharest passed the quarantine line without being searched. At 10:30 Stevenson lays a sheet of paper on your desk. It is a single unsigned page whose four points seem to have been written in Washington, and he asks you to send it to Khrushchev as “the Secretary-General’s own proposal.” The United States has not yet answered yesterday’s first appeal, yet it wants a second one first. Bunche says that if you take this paper, the Secretary-General becomes Washington’s postman. Loutfi says it is the only door through which the Soviets can retreat and save face. Khrushchev’s answer to the first appeal has not come. You expect Zorin to attack the legality of the blockade at length at the 4 p.m. meeting.

voices.who: Last night’s meeting with Zorin (as you described it to Stevenson this morning; Stevenson’s record)
voices.text: Thant told me Zorin had come to see him at 7:30 last night and asked what appeal SYG would make in the Council. Thant replied it would be based on his appeal to Khrushchev and Kennedy. Zorin said he had not received it. When Thant explained its nature, Zorin replied it was a very bad proposal since the blockade was entirely illegal; Thant should concern himself with legality and should not put lifting of the quarantine on the same basis as stopping shipments to Cuba. Thant replied he was not concerned with legality but with avoiding a crisis.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary)
voices.text: Send these four points as they stand, and Moscow will know who wrote them. Zorin was so angry last night because he thought the Secretary-General had leaned toward the Americans. Hold to the freeze you proposed in the first appeal. That is why the non-aligned stand behind you.

voices.who: Omar Loutfi (under-secretary)
voices.text: Secretary-General, there are reports that some Soviet ships have turned around since yesterday. To stop the rest of them, Khrushchev needs a request from the UN, not from Kennedy. The sentences on this paper are American, but the signature is yours. For the Soviets, that signature is a door.

choices.text: Rewrite the four points in the Secretary-General’s own words without changing their meaning, and send them at 2:26 p.m. to Khrushchev through Zorin, and separately to Kennedy
choices.why: Whoever wrote it, if the ships stop at sea, the mediator has won
choices.after: Kennedy’s reply to the first appeal came in at 2:19 p.m., Khrushchev’s at 3:30. Khrushchev wrote, “I agree with your proposal.” At the 4 p.m. meeting Stevenson demanded a “yes or no” from Zorin, and Zorin answered that he was not in an American courtroom. At 7:25 p.m., on a motion by the UAR and Ghana, the Council adjourned without setting a date.

choices.text: Send nothing until Khrushchev’s answer to the first appeal arrives. Read it, then write the second appeal late in the afternoon
choices.why: A mediator who writes the next letter before getting an answer loses trust
choices.after: Khrushchev’s answer came at 3:30: “I agree with your proposal.” At 5 you sent the second appeal, asking the ships to wait outside the interception line, and Stevenson learned of it just before the meeting. In the meantime no search at sea was announced.

choices.text: Refuse to pass on the American draft. Hold to the two-to-three-week freeze of the first appeal, and wait with the non-aligned delegates for the two leaders’ answers
choices.why: The moment you carry one side’s text, you are no longer fit to mediate
choices.after: Stevenson folded the paper and put it away without a word. At 3:30 Khrushchev’s answer to the first appeal came: “I agree with your proposal.” The Soviet Union had accepted the freeze, and the United States had not yet answered. Now the ball was in your court.

note.text: This one-page memorandum was found in the UN archives in the 2000s, with “Handed to the Acting Secretary-General by Stevenson, 10:30 a.m., 25 October” written by hand in the margin. Its text matches the four points of State Department cable No. 1084, which Rusk sent at 2 a.m. The second appeal went out at 2:26 p.m.; the American reply to the first appeal had gone seven minutes earlier, at 2:19. The memorandum is given here as Dorn and Pauk reproduce it, checked against the original in FRUS XI d69.

pressure.title: The Postman
pressure.text: The paper Stevenson handed you at 10:30 is unsigned, and its four points read like Washington’s own sentences. At 7:30 the evening before, Zorin had called your first appeal a very bad proposal and said you should take up the illegality of the blockade; you replied that you were concerned not with legality but with averting a crisis. The United States has not answered the first appeal yet demands the second one first, so Bunche sees that taking this paper would mean the Secretary-General carrying Washington’s words under his own name; Loutfi sees it as the Soviets’ only door to retreat with their dignity intact. Khrushchev has not answered yet, and how Moscow read your first appeal you can only guess from Zorin’s anger. Only a few people in this room know who wrote this paper, and if the ships stop at sea, they will be answering a request made in your name.

map.caption: The quarantine line runs through the waters around Cuba. Where the Soviet ships are now, you can learn only from American announcements.

UT-03.unknown: The four points Stevenson handed you were word for word the text of State Department cable No. 1084, which Rusk had sent to New York at 2 a.m. The American first reply went out at 2:19 p.m., seven minutes ahead of your second appeal, and that same day ExComm spent two hours deciding whether to stop an East German passenger ship. For years no one knew that the Americans had drafted the appeal; this one-page memorandum turned up in the UN archives in the 2000s. The next morning Khrushchev sent his second reply, saying he had ordered the Soviet ships to stay outside the interception area.

UT-04.title: Modalities
UT-04.clock: About a day until the Soviet ship Grozny is expected at the quarantine line, by the American account

telegram.from: N. Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.to: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.subject: Reply to your message of 25 October
telegram.text: Dear U Thant, I have received and studied your message of 25 October. I understand your concern for the preservation of peace and highly appreciate your efforts to avert military conflict. / I therefore accept your proposal, and have ordered the masters of Soviet vessels bound for Cuba but not yet within the area of the American warships’ piratical activities to stay out of the interception area, as you recommend. / But we have given this order in the hope that the other side will understand that such a situation, in which we keep vessels immobilized on the high seas, must be a purely temporary one; the period cannot under any circumstances be of long duration. / I thank you for your efforts and wish you success in your noble task.

UT-04.event: At yesterday’s 1025th meeting, at 4 p.m., Stevenson demanded of Zorin, in the president’s chair, a “yes or no”: had the Soviet Union installed medium- and intermediate-range missiles in Cuba? Zorin answered that he was not in an American courtroom. Stevenson said he would wait for an answer “until hell freezes over” and set up his photographs in the chamber. This morning Khrushchev’s second reply came: Soviet ships will stay outside the interception area, but only as something “purely temporary.” Yesterday Kennedy replied that if the Soviets complied, American warships would avoid a confrontation, but added that work inside Cuba was continuing. At 7:50 this morning, the U.S. Navy announced, an American destroyer boarded the Lebanese freighter Marucla, the first ship to be searched.
UT-04.scene: The sea has stopped. But Stevenson says photographs come in every day showing work going on at the bases in Cuba under lights through the night. Today you see Zorin and Stevenson separately to discuss “modalities.” Stevenson says the quarantine can be lifted only after arms shipments and base construction have stopped and that has been verified, and he raises a plan for the UN to inspect ships bound for Cuba, at sea or in Cuban ports. Zorin says the halt in shipments and the lifting of the blockade must happen at the same time, and that inspection is a matter for the Cuban government. Neither man can speak for Cuba. Yesterday, through García-Incháustegui, Cuba denounced the blockade as an act of war, but it has not yet answered your appeal of the 24th. To write directly to Havana would be for the Secretary-General to ask a member government to stop work on military installations on its own soil, and there is no precedent for that.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson to Zorin (1025th meeting, yesterday)
voices.text: Do you, Ambassador Zorin, deny that the USSR has placed and is placing medium- and intermediate-range missiles and sites in Cuba? Yes or no? Don’t wait for the translation. Yes or no?

voices.who: Valerian Zorin (president of the Council, in Russian) to Stevenson
voices.text: I am not in an American courtroom, sir, and therefore I do not wish to answer a question that is put to me in the fashion in which a prosecutor does. In due course, sir, you will have your answer as the Soviet representative.

voices.who: Mario García-Incháustegui (Cuban permanent representative, 1025th meeting, yesterday)
voices.text: The representative of the United States has offered no serious evidence in support of his President’s claim that Cuba constitutes a nuclear threat to the countries of the Western Hemisphere. The weapons Cuba possesses are of an entirely defensive character. They are weapons Cuba has been obliged to acquire because of the aggressive and interventionist policy of the United States Government toward Cuba.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (meeting today)
voices.text: Secretary-General, stopping the ships is a first step. But the concrete is setting at the bases. The quarantine cannot be lifted until the work stops and the UN has verified it. The UN could inspect the ships, at sea or in port.

choices.text: Reconvene the Security Council and turn the two sides’ agreement on “modalities” into a resolution. A Council document carries more weight than a letter from the Secretary-General
choices.why: A Secretary-General’s letter can be refused, but a Council resolution stays on the record
choices.after: As president, Zorin agreed to call a meeting but refused to have “a halt to construction inside Cuba” in the text, and Stevenson said that without it he would vote against. The meeting never took place. When night came you wrote to Havana after all. A day had gone by.

choices.text: Write directly to Castro, citing what Dorticós said on 8 October, and ask that construction of missile launch facilities be halted while negotiations go on
choices.why: What the two great powers have stopped at sea must also be stopped on the ground in Cuba
choices.after: The letter went to Havana that day through García-Incháustegui. You wrote that you had received “fairly encouraging replies” from the two leaders, and asked that construction of “installations designed to launch medium-range and intermediate-range ballistic missiles” be suspended during the negotiations. No answer came from Havana that night.

choices.text: Recast Stevenson’s ship-inspection plan as the Secretary-General’s own and put it to Zorin first. Once inspection is in place, there is a case for lifting the quarantine
choices.why: Build a framework for verification first, and both sides gain room to step back
choices.after: Zorin answered the next day: inspection of Soviet ships was a matter for the Cuban government. Cuba did not answer. That night you wrote to Havana, without a single line about inspection.

note.text: Khrushchev’s first reply of the 25th (“I agree with your proposal”) was made public at the 1025th meeting of the Security Council, and his second reply of the 26th in press release SG/1357. For Kennedy’s replies of the 25th and 26th, this research could confirm the full text only through FRUS editorial notes (excerpt). The U.S. Navy announced the same day that the Marucla had been boarded at 7:50 a.m. (Eastern Daylight Time) on the 26th.
