UT-04.unknown: At that hour reconnaissance photographs reaching Washington every day showed work at the bases in Cuba going on through the night. In Havana on the night of the 26th, Castro sat at the Soviet embassy until dawn writing a letter to Khrushchev.

UT-05.title: An Invitation on Black Saturday
UT-05.clock: 9 hours since Radio Moscow’s new letter. No answer yet from Washington

telegram.kind: Letter (English translation of the Spanish original)
telegram.from: Fidel Castro Ruz, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba (through Permanent Representative García-Incháustegui)
telegram.to: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.subject: Reply to your message of 26 October
telegram.text: Your Excellency, I have received your message dated 26 October, and I express to you my appreciation of your noble concern. / Cuba is prepared to discuss as fully as may be necessary its differences with the United States and to do everything in its power, in cooperation with the United Nations, to resolve the present crisis. However, it flatly rejects the violation of the sovereignty of our country involved in the naval blockade, an act of force and war committed by the United States against Cuba. / The Revolutionary Government of Cuba would be prepared to accept the compromises that you request as efforts in favor of peace, provided that at the same time, while negotiations are in progress, the United States Government desists from threats and aggressive actions against Cuba, including the naval blockade of our country. / Furthermore, should you consider it useful to the cause of peace, our Government would be glad to receive you in our country, as Secretary-General of the United Nations, with a view to direct discussions on the present crisis. / Cuba can do whatever is asked of it, except to agree to be a victim or to renounce the rights that belong to every sovereign state.
telegram.sign: Major Fidel Castro Ruz, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba

UT-05.event: At 10 a.m. Radio Moscow read out a new letter from Khrushchev: a public offer to trade the missiles in Cuba for the missiles in Turkey. In the afternoon word reached New York that an American reconnaissance plane had been shot down over Cuba. Stevenson will not say how Washington means to answer either. Meanwhile García-Incháustegui has laid Castro’s reply on your desk.
UT-05.scene: Castro rejects the blockade and rejects any right of the United States to decide how Cuba is armed, yet he writes that he will accept the “compromises” you asked for if the blockade is lifted at the same time, and at the end he asks you to come to Havana. There is not a word about inspection. The Brazilian delegation reports that its ambassador in Havana thinks that silence “may be a sign of softening.” Bunche says that if you go to Havana now, the agenda will be the lifting of the blockade, not the withdrawal of the missiles, and the Secretary-General will be Cuba’s guest. Loutfi says that if you do not go to Cuba, there is nothing at all the UN can do on Cuban soil. Stevenson has telephoned for a copy. If you accept the invitation, you will be the first secretary-general since Hammarskjöld to go to the scene of a crisis; if you decline, you will be the man in New York waiting for the two powers to make their deal.

voices.who: U Thant to Castro (letter of yesterday)
voices.text: I do not know whether Ambassador García has reported to you, but I have received fairly encouraging replies from the President of the United States and the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR to my appeal for negotiations and a peaceful settlement of the problem. Your Excellency could make a significant contribution to the peace of the world at this present critical juncture by directing that the construction and development of major military facilities and installations in Cuba, and especially installations designed to launch medium-range and intermediate-range ballistic missiles, be suspended during the period of negotiations which are now under way.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary)
voices.text: There is no inspection in this letter. There is only the condition that he will compromise once the blockade is lifted. If you go, the talks will open on Castro’s agenda. Accept, but put off leaving until an agreement between Washington and Moscow is in sight.

voices.who: Omar Loutfi (under-secretary)
voices.text: Secretary-General, if you simply go to Havana, the Americans cannot bomb for those few days. And Cuba will find it hard to fire on American planes during those days. Those few days are the time the two capitals need.

voices.who: The Brazilian delegation (New York, passing on its Havana ambassador’s view)
voices.text: Our ambassador in Havana thinks that the absence of any rejection of inspection in Castro’s reply may be a sign of softening. Brazil is ready to help the Secretary-General visit Havana, and then to put the denuclearization of Latin America on the agenda.

choices.text: Decline to go to Havana. The Secretary-General stays in New York to protect the framework of the U.S.–Soviet negotiations, and deals with Cuba through its two ambassadors, Lechuga and García
choices.why: A mediator who enters one side’s capital loses the other side’s trust
choices.after: Your answer was courteous, but Castro read it as a refusal. The next morning Radio Moscow announced the withdrawal, and the Secretary-General was left to deal with inspection without a foothold anywhere in Cuba.

choices.text: Say you are willing to accept the invitation, and send Stevenson a copy. Tomorrow, write to the three governments confirming what has been agreed
choices.why: Unless the UN gets onto Cuban soil, any agreement will stall there
choices.after: Late that night the White House released the President’s reply to Khrushchev. Stevenson, on receiving the copy, said he would come up at 10 the next morning. No one told you what Moscow would do that night.

choices.text: Take up this morning’s public letter from Khrushchev and prepare to put forward the simultaneous removal of the missiles in Cuba and Turkey as the Secretary-General’s proposal
choices.why: A deal both sides have already named saves face for both if a third party proposes it
choices.after: Loutfi began writing a draft. After 10 p.m. an unexpected call came. It was Andrew Cordier of Columbia University. The man who had been Hammarskjöld’s under-secretary said he had to see the Secretary-General that night.

note.text: That same night in Washington, Rusk telephoned Cordier at Columbia University and dictated a statement putting forward “the simultaneous removal of the missiles in Cuba and Turkey” as U Thant’s proposal, telling him to hold it and hand it to the Secretary-General only on a further signal. The signal never came, and U Thant never knew. The episode came to light only when Rusk revealed it in a letter in 1987. Castro’s reply was written in Spanish; the text here follows the English translation in the UN press release.

pressure.title: “Come to Havana”
pressure.text: Castro’s reply rejects the blockade and the premise that the United States has a right to decide how Cuba is armed, yet it says he is ready to accept the compromise you asked for if, while negotiations go on, threats and acts of aggression, the blockade included, cease; and at the end it says the Cuban government would be glad to receive you. Your letter to Havana of 26 October had no precedent: it asked a member government to stop work on military installations on its own soil, and it did so by quoting Dorticós’s speech of 8 October, handing Cuba’s own words back to Cuba. Today word came that an American reconnaissance plane had been shot down over Cuba, and how Washington will answer that, and the morning’s broadcast from Moscow, is still unknown. Hammarskjöld flew toward the scene of a crisis in September 1961 and never came back; if you accept, you will be the first secretary-general since then to go to the scene of one. How you answer an invitation that says nothing about inspection will decide whether the man who goes to Havana is seen as a mediator or as Cuba’s guest.

UT-05.unknown: At that hour in Washington, ExComm argued for three hours from 4 p.m. over the reply to Khrushchev; at 7:45 p.m. Robert Kennedy met Ambassador Dobrynin, and at 8:05 p.m. Kennedy’s reply went out to Moscow. The letter broadcast that morning set different terms from Khrushchev’s private letter (withdrawal in return for a no-invasion pledge), which had reached Washington on the night of the 26th. The U-2 came down over Banes at 11:20 a.m., Washington time, killing its pilot, Major Anderson, and in the Caribbean American destroyers were dropping practice depth charges on a Soviet submarine. The reading of Castro’s silence as a sign of softening came from the Brazilian ambassador’s report home from Havana. That same night Rusk dictated to Cordier at Columbia a statement in which U Thant would propose removing the missiles in Cuba and Turkey together, and had him hold it; the signal to release it never came.

UT-06.title: The Sunday Morning Broadcast
UT-06.clock: 48 hours until departure for Havana (10 a.m., 30 October)

telegram.from: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.to: Fidel Castro, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba (through Permanent Representative García-Incháustegui)
telegram.subject: Reply to your letter of 27 October
telegram.text: Your Excellency, I have the honor to acknowledge with deep appreciation the receipt of your kind letter of 27 October. I was particularly gratified to note that the Revolutionary Government of Cuba would be prepared to accept the compromises that I requested as efforts in favor of peace, provided that at the same time, while negotiations are in progress, the United States Government desists from threats and aggressive actions against Cuba, including the naval blockade. / I gladly accept your invitation, and I hope to leave early next week. I would like to take some of my aides with me, some of whom I would wish to leave behind to continue our joint efforts toward a peaceful solution of the problem. / I note and appreciate your view that full respect for the sovereignty of Cuba is an essential prerequisite for any solution of the problem. / I hope that as a result of these discussions a solution may be reached by which the principle of respect for the sovereignty of Cuba will be assured, and that it may also be possible for action to be taken which would reassure other countries which have felt themselves threatened by recent developments in Cuba.

UT-06.event: At 10 a.m. Radio Moscow read out yet another letter from Khrushchev. The weapons “described as offensive” would be dismantled, crated and returned to the Soviet Union, and UN representatives could verify the dismantling. In the afternoon Kennedy issued a statement welcoming “a statesmanlike decision.” The same day in Havana, Castro announced five conditions: an end to the economic blockade, to subversive activities, to pirate attacks, and to violations of Cuban airspace and waters, and the return of Guantánamo. Yesterday and today alike, Cuba has avoided the word inspection.
UT-06.scene: Stevenson and Yost have come up at 10. You have decided to write separately to each of the three governments. To Khrushchev, you welcome the dispatch of First Deputy Foreign Minister Kuznetsov to New York and propose to discuss the form of supervision; to Kennedy, you confirm the two conditions of his letter of 27 October (removal under UN supervision, and in return the lifting of the quarantine and an assurance against invasion) and say you will pass them on to Castro; to Castro, you accept the invitation and say you will leave early next week. Brigadier Rikhye proposes taking six to ten military technicians from neutral countries such as Ethiopia and Sweden and leaving them on the spot, and he is arranging a neutral aircraft (a Royal Canadian Air Force plane or a Brazilian airliner) and an independent communications link. Stevenson warns against leaving early, saying that if you go before an inspection team is formed you will come back empty-handed; coming back in the evening, he answered your request that the quarantine be publicly suspended on the 30th and reconnaissance halted during your visit with “verification arrangements first.” You think there is no chance the Soviets will fire missiles in the next two or three days, and you have expressed deep concern at yesterday’s call-up of 14,000 Air Force reservists.

voices.who: U Thant to Kennedy (through Stevenson, letter of today)
voices.text: Mr. Stevenson also handed to me a copy of your letter of 27 October to Chairman Khrushchev. I am very gratified by your spirit of cooperation and concern for peace. I note in particular that in this letter you state: 1. You [the USSR] would agree to remove these weapons systems from Cuba under appropriate United Nations observation and supervision, and undertake, with suitable safeguards, to halt the further introduction of such weapons systems into Cuba. 2. We, on our part, would agree, upon the establishment of adequate arrangements through the United Nations, (a) to remove promptly the quarantine measures now in effect and (b) to give assurances against an invasion of Cuba.

voices.who: Your words to Stevenson (this evening; Stevenson’s record)
voices.text: In response to the U.S. position that verification arrangements must be approved and in place before the blockade is suspended, SYG said he saw no possibility whatever that the Soviets would fire missiles at the United States in the next two or three days. To do so would be obvious suicide for the USSR and Cuba. He expressed deep concern at yesterday’s call-up of Air Force reserves.

voices.who: C. V. Narasimhan (chef de cabinet)
voices.text: Castro is certain to bring up American subversion and Guantánamo. Stevenson wants all of that kept out of these negotiations, but leave it out in Havana and the talks will be over in two hours.

choices.text: Take Stevenson’s advice and delay your departure; go into Havana once Rikhye has assembled an inspection team of military technicians from neutral countries, and take them with you
choices.why: A mediator who goes without the means to verify has nothing to say when he returns
choices.after: Sweden and Ethiopia said they would send men; India asked for another day. Meanwhile, on the 29th, American reconnaissance planes flew over Cuba again and Cuban batteries fired on them. On the day the words “inspection team” appeared in the papers, you cabled to ask whether the invitation still stood, and García-Incháustegui did not reply.

choices.text: Leave on the morning of the 30th. Take only Loutfi, Tavares de Sá and Rikhye, and settle the question of an inspection team with Castro himself in Havana
choices.why: An inspection team without Cuba’s consent is only a piece of paper, so meet the man first
choices.after: Kuznetsov came on the afternoon of the 29th. The Soviet Union agreed to have the Red Cross inspect Soviet ships bound for Cuba but refused inspection of ships by a UN team, and said inspection in Cuban ports was “up to Cuba.” On the night of the 29th the White House announced that “at the request of the Secretary-General” it was voluntarily suspending enforcement of the quarantine for the duration of his visit, and word came that reconnaissance flights would also stop on the 30th and 31st.

choices.text: Make a public suspension of the American blockade and a halt to reconnaissance during your visit the conditions of going. Tell Stevenson that if they are not accepted, you will not go
choices.why: American planes must not fly over the head of a Secretary-General entering Cuba
choices.after: On the morning of the 30th word came that the President had agreed to halt reconnaissance and suspend enforcement of the quarantine for two days. You got your conditions, and in return the United States settled down to watch what the Secretary-General would bring back.

note.text: In his talks with Kuznetsov on the 29th, U Thant worried whether the word “continuation” in Kennedy’s letter of 27 October meant open-ended inspection; if so, he said, Castro would demand inspection of “CIA exile training camps in the United States and the Caribbean.” The Americans replied that it did not mean open-ended inspection. That day Rusk approved the text of a statement suspending the quarantine for two days, and on the 30th Kennedy halted reconnaissance for those two days. The plan for six to ten military technicians from neutral countries and a neutral aircraft (an RCAF plane or a Brazilian airliner) appears in a U.S. Mission cable of 28 October; in the event, a chartered Brazilian Varig plane was used.
note.src: FRUS XI d112; FRUS XI d113; FRUS XI d114; FRUS Supp d445; SG/1364·1365

UT-06.unknown: At that hour in Havana, Castro first heard of Khrushchev’s decision on the radio. In his report to Washington that evening, Stevenson wrote that the Secretary-General, though he did not say so explicitly, left the impression that he regarded some U.S. actions as excessive. On the 29th Rusk approved the text of a statement suspending the quarantine for two days; on the morning of the 30th he told ExComm that the Secretary-General had said he would not go if reconnaissance continued, and Kennedy halted reconnaissance for those two days.

UT-07.place: Presidential Palace, Havana: the conference room
UT-07.title: Demands Fit for a Conquered Country
UT-07.clock: A little over a day until the flight back to New York (evening of 31 October)

telegram.kind: Press release (UN information officer, from Havana)
telegram.from: UN Office of Public Information (information officer traveling with the Acting Secretary-General)
telegram.subject: Acting Secretary-General opens talks in Cuba
telegram.text: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations, and his party arrived in Havana from New York at 1:15 p.m. today aboard a chartered Varig airliner. / At the airport the Acting Secretary-General and his party were met by Raúl Roa, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Cuba; Pelegrín Torras, Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs; General Albino Silva, special envoy of the President of Brazil; Luiz Bastian Pinto, Ambassador of Brazil in Havana; and Abdel Moneim El-Shinnawi, chargé d’affaires of the United Arab Republic in Cuba. / The Acting Secretary-General began his first official talks at 3:10 p.m. at the Presidential Palace in Havana. / Present on the Cuban side were President Osvaldo Dorticós, Prime Minister Fidel Castro and Foreign Minister Raúl Roa; on the Secretary-General’s side, Under-Secretaries Omar Loutfi and Hernane Tavares de Sá and his military adviser, Brigadier I. J. Rikhye.

UT-07.event: On the 29th the front page of the Havana paper Revolución carried the headline “Khrushchev Orders Rockets Withdrawn from Cuba” alongside the five conditions. The Cuban government has added nothing to its declaration of the 27th that it will not tolerate military aircraft violating its airspace. In New York Kuznetsov put forward the Red Cross plan for inspecting ships, and Washington has suspended enforcement of the quarantine and reconnaissance flights for the two days you are in Cuba. The skies over Cuba are quiet.
UT-07.scene: In the conference room of the Presidential Palace sit Dorticós, Castro and Roa. You ask where Cuba stands on Red Cross inspection of ships, and you pass on three American proposals: ground verification by a UN team for two or three weeks, UN reconnaissance aircraft, or reconnaissance aircraft carrying Cuban, Soviet and American crews together. Then you convey the American offer of a public pledge not to invade and a promise to lift the blockade. Castro answers at length and with heat. Inspection, he says, is something that can be imposed only on a conquered country; there can be no inspection in the ports either, and the immediate agenda is the five conditions. Dorticós asks whether the danger of war lies in Cuba’s weapons or in America’s intent to invade. His words carry anger not only at the United States but at the Soviet Union, which seems to have decided on withdrawal without consulting Cuba. You want to leave two or three UN representatives in Havana, and the United States wants Major Anderson’s body back. Tomorrow’s second session will be private.

voices.who: Fidel Castro (Presidential Palace, transcript of the first session, 30 October)
voices.text: What right does the United States have to ask this? I mean, is it based on a real right, or is it a demand based on force, on a position of strength? Cuba is not Austria, nor the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia, nor the Congo. Cuba has the firmest determination to defend its rights. Cuba cannot accept demands that can be imposed only on a conquered country. They would first have to destroy us, to wipe us out, and in any case they will not find here anyone on whom to impose humiliating terms.
voices.src: Castro 1962-11-02 CMQ broadcast (English translation of the 10/30 transcript)

voices.who: Osvaldo Dorticós (president)
voices.text: Where does the danger of war lie? In this or that weapon Cuba has, or in the aggressive intentions of the United States toward Cuba? Why should inspection, the acceptance of inspection, be the condition for guaranteeing peace?
voices.src: Castro 1962-11-02 CMQ broadcast (English translation of the 10/30 transcript)

voices.who: Brigadier I. J. Rikhye (military adviser, after the session)
voices.text: Secretary-General, you could see on the road from the airport that Soviet troops are taking the bases apart. Even if Cuba refuses inspection, the dismantling is a fact. Going back with that fact and going back saying we failed to get inspection are the same thing told two different ways.

voices.who: Omar Loutfi (under-secretary)
voices.text: The Americans in New York will never accept the five conditions. But ask to take them off the agenda here, and the talks are over. Hear them out, and promise nothing.

choices.text: Of the three American proposals, press for UN reconnaissance aircraft as a condition, and do not drop your demand to leave UN staff behind. An agreement without inspection is no agreement
choices.why: Winning Cuba’s consent is why the Secretary-General came here
choices.after: At the second session Castro said the same things at greater length. Not one UN staff member was allowed to stay. You came back with nothing but the return of Anderson’s body. The New York papers wrote that the Secretary-General had come back empty-handed.

choices.text: Do not force inspection. Get confirmation that dismantling is under way and the return of Anderson’s body, and in tomorrow’s private session quietly take up the airspace issue and the wording of Castro’s speech
choices.why: Rather than fight over what you cannot get today, take what you can
choices.after: At the private session on the morning of the 31st, Castro demanded an end to violations of Cuban airspace, agreed to return the body, and refused to let UN staff remain. When you asked him to drop the passage rejecting inspection from his speech of 1 November, he agreed. At Idlewild you called the talks “useful” and said the dismantling would be finished by Friday.

choices.text: Promise to take the five conditions back to New York as items for the U.S.–Soviet agenda. Only when Cuba is on the agenda will inspection follow
choices.why: Cuba must be made a party to the negotiations before anything inside Cuba can be settled
choices.after: For the first time, Castro smiled. But on the evening of 1 November in New York, when Mikoyan proposed linking the five conditions to the U.S.–Soviet agreement, Stevenson and McCloy replied “one issue only,” and the promise the Secretary-General had made in Havana became an argument for the Soviet side.

note.text: U Thant’s own record of the Havana talks has never been released; the transcript of the first session is known because Castro read it out on CMQ television on 2 November. The second session remains private. The Yugoslav ambassador’s report (30 October) and cables from the Czechoslovak and Polish embassies convey the mood on the Cuban side. Daylight saving time ended in the United States on 28 October, putting New York and Havana on the same time; Moscow is eight hours ahead of New York.

pressure.title: The Anger in That Room
pressure.text: You landed in Havana at 1:15 p.m. today, and the talks at the Presidential Palace began at 3:10 p.m. With you are Loutfi, Tavares de Sá and Brigadier Rikhye; the six to ten military technicians from neutral countries that Stevenson wanted did not come. Yesterday Kuznetsov proposed that the Red Cross inspect Soviet ships bound for Cuba; you thought inspection in Cuban ports would be easier, and the United States agreed to a short statement suspending the blockade for the duration of your visit. When Castro asks where America gets the right to demand this, the anger in the room is directed not only at the United States but at the Soviet Union, which seems to have decided on withdrawal without consulting him, and it is aimed not at the proposals you carry but at the very seat you occupy. What you can say you got when you return to New York depends on tomorrow’s private session.
pressure.src: SG/1364·1365; SG/1368; FRUS XI d112; Castro 1962-11-02 CMQ broadcast (English translation of the 10/30 transcript); Wilson/UMD 115474

map.caption: You landed in Havana on the afternoon of 30 October and began talks with Castro at the Presidential Palace.

UT-07.unknown: At that hour Castro had already replied to Khrushchev, on the evening of the 28th: he would order the anti-aircraft batteries to hold their fire, but only while negotiations went on, and would not withdraw the declaration of the 27th that violations of Cuban airspace would not be tolerated; and he wrote that Cuba was “opposed in principle to inspection of its territory.” Moscow had decided on withdrawal without telling Cuba, and Castro heard the news on the radio on the 28th. After the talks the Yugoslav ambassador reported home that “Fidel was very stubborn and accepted nothing.”

UT-08.title: Verification, Not Inspection
UT-08.clock: Mikoyan’s second week in Havana. No date yet for lifting the blockade

telegram.from: Fidel Castro, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba (through Permanent Representative Lechuga)
telegram.to: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.subject: Violations of Cuban airspace by U.S. military aircraft, and the question of inspection
telegram.text: As Cuba has informed you and has publicly reiterated, it does not accept unilateral inspection of Cuban territory by any body, national or international. / On 27 October, in the midst of the crisis, the Government of Cuba declared that it would never recognize the privilege of any warplane to violate Cuban airspace. / Our airspace and our sovereignty will never be a matter for negotiation. / Any warplane that enters Cuban airspace and violates our sovereignty must run the risk of being shot down within range of our anti-aircraft weapons.

UT-08.event: On 1 November Mikoyan, passing through New York on his way to Havana, saw you and demanded an immediate end to the blockade. That evening he met Stevenson and McCloy separately at the Soviet mission, and since then, you hear, the American and Soviet delegates have been settling the missile count and how to check it at sea, outside the Secretary-General’s office. On 8 November the Red Cross withdrew from ship inspection, saying “its statutes do not permit it.” Mikoyan has now spent two weeks in Havana trying to persuade Castro, and the question of withdrawing the Il-28 bombers has newly arisen. Today Castro’s letter came, and American low-level reconnaissance has resumed.
UT-08.scene: All 42 missiles have gone out to sea, and the U.S. Navy has photographed them from alongside the ships. But inside Cuba the UN has not verified anything, not once, and the “verification by UN representatives” Khrushchev promised on 28 October exists only on paper. On the 6th Brazil’s Arinos proposed that the neutral ambassadors in Havana view the sites as a group, and you decided to pass it on to the Americans as the Secretary-General’s proposal. Since the 12th you have been saying “verification” rather than “inspection.” The Soviets and Cubans together circulated a 12-article draft protocol, but Stevenson said he could not accept it because it contains the five conditions. You have three options left: keep a “mobile verification team” of neutral personnel at headquarters in New York and send it when needed; close the matter with separate declarations by the United States, the Soviet Union and the Secretary-General in the Security Council; or form a verification team without Cuba’s consent and push it through with a Council resolution. Lechuga says “it is important that the UN not lose control,” and Stevenson is furious about Castro’s letter. The Americans and Soviets are already meeting on their own.

voices.who: Vasily Kuznetsov (Soviet first deputy foreign minister, 29 October)
voices.text: Since the United States is concerned about offensive weapons going to Cuba, the Soviet Union is prepared to agree to a proposal that the Red Cross board Soviet ships bound for Cuba to verify that they carry no weapons.

voices.who: Anastas Mikoyan (Soviet first deputy premier, talks with the Americans on the evening of 1 November, as Stevenson relayed them)
voices.text: Cuba is an independent country, and the Soviet Union does not control those batteries. We cannot guarantee that those anti-aircraft guns will not fire. Castro’s five conditions are “fundamental questions” that cannot be separated from the U.S.–Soviet agreement, and the agreement must be given proper form as a document registered with the UN.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative)
voices.text: Secretary-General, there will be no verification inside Cuba now. The United States counted the missiles at sea, and that is enough. What remains is the Il-28s and a date for lifting the blockade, and we will settle that with Kuznetsov, just the two of us. Don’t answer Castro’s letter.

voices.who: Carlos Lechuga (Cuban permanent representative, his own record)
voices.text: Once the Americans and the Soviets start meeting on their own, neither Cuba nor the UN is in the room. It is important that the UN not lose control. Cuba can talk to the Secretary-General.

choices.text: Form a verification team of neutral personnel without Cuba’s consent and push its dispatch through with a Security Council resolution. Get Khrushchev’s promise of 28 October down on paper
choices.why: If the promised UN verification is abandoned, the UN’s word will carry no weight in the next crisis
choices.after: Rikhye drew up a list of Swedish, Ethiopian, Indian and Brazilian officers in a single day. Lechuga, hearing of the resolution, cabled Havana that evening, and Zorin said the resolution would “put Cuba’s sovereignty to a vote in the Security Council.”

choices.text: Give up on verification inside Cuba. Tacitly accept the U.S. Navy’s checks at sea, and close the matter with separate declarations by the United States, the Soviet Union and the Secretary-General in the Security Council
choices.why: Better to set up a procedure that can end this than fight over an inspection that cannot happen
choices.after: On the 19th Castro wrote to you that the Il-28s were Soviet property and that he would not object if the Soviet Union thought it desirable to withdraw them. At 6 p.m. on the 20th Kennedy told a press conference that Khrushchev had informed him the bombers would be out within a month, and announced that the blockade was lifted. The three declarations reached the Security Council only on 7 January 1963, as a joint letter, and the UN never once got inside Cuba after that.

choices.text: Propose to the United States, the Soviet Union and Cuba at once a mobile verification team, kept at headquarters in New York and sent only at the request of both Cuba and the United States
choices.why: The mere existence of a verification team becomes a framework for the next crisis
choices.after: The United States said it would “study” the idea, the Soviet Union welcomed it, and Cuba did not reply. The team remained on paper. On 20 November Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade, and on 7 January 1963 the United States and the Soviet Union sent the Security Council a joint letter and had the matter taken off the agenda. The UN never once got inside Cuba after that.

note.text: Khrushchev’s letter of 28 October promised that “UN representatives could verify the dismantling,” but Cuba refused, so UN verification on the spot never took place; the U.S. Navy’s counting of the departing missiles at sea took its place. Castro’s letter of 15 November was delivered through Ambassador Lechuga; the Cuban forces’ authorization of anti-aircraft fire on 17 November and its withdrawal on the 18th are confirmed only by the titles of documents.
note.src: FRUS XI d133; FRUS XI d142; SG/1378; SG/1379; Wilson/UMD 91339

UT-08.unknown: Meanwhile, at the Soviet mission in New York on the evening of 1 November, Mikoyan argued for four hours with Stevenson and McCloy over linking the five conditions; the Americans replied “one issue only,” and the Soviets said they “could not guarantee that Cuban anti-aircraft guns, which are beyond their control, would not fire.” On 4 November McCloy and Kuznetsov confirmed the figures (as of 22 October, 24 launch sites completed and 16 unfinished, and 42 missiles, all rendered inoperable on 2 November) and discussed having American warships check the missiles at sea by sight and photograph. In Havana two days later, on 17 November, the Cuban forces authorized anti-aircraft fire, and they withdrew the order the next day.

UT-H1.title: The Burden of the Freeze
UT-H1.clock: About a day until the Soviet ship Grozny is expected at the quarantine line, by the American account
UT-H1.event: At 3:30 p.m. on the 25th Khrushchev’s answer came: “I agree with your proposal.” The Soviet Union had agreed to a freeze of two to three weeks. In its reply at 2:19 that afternoon, the United States wrote that the cause of the crisis was the offensive weapons secretly brought into Cuba and that the answer was their removal, and said only that it had instructed Stevenson to hold “preliminary talks.” Yesterday morning the tanker Bucharest passed without being searched, and so did an East German passenger ship. This morning an American destroyer boarded the Lebanese freighter Marucla. The White House has announced that work at the bases in Cuba is not stopping.
UT-H1.scene: The mood outside the chamber is on your side. Delegates of about 50 Asian, African and Arab countries are preparing to call an emergency special session of the General Assembly to back the Secretary-General’s freeze, and Riad says it now looks as though the United States alone is rejecting a plan the Soviets have accepted. But the Americans say they cannot accept a freeze that does not halt construction inside Cuba, and Stevenson has not telephoned since you refused yesterday’s four points. Zorin has come again to say it is now time for the Security Council to take up the legality of the blockade formally. Bunche says that if this goes to the General Assembly, the two powers will bypass the UN and start talking to each other directly. Loutfi says that if the Secretary-General withdraws a plan the Soviets have accepted, the non-aligned will abandon him. At sea, the Grozny is heading for the interception line.

voices.who: Nikita Khrushchev to U Thant (first answer, 25 October)
voices.text: I have received your message and have carefully studied the proposal it contains. I welcome your initiative. The Soviet Government, too, considers the situation in the Caribbean highly dangerous and requiring immediate intervention by the United Nations. I wish to inform you that I agree with your proposal, which is in the interest of peace.

voices.who: Mahmoud Riad (United Arab Republic)
voices.text: Secretary-General, one side has agreed and the other is silent. If nearly 50 countries convene the General Assembly to back the freeze, the United States will have to answer before world opinion. The General Assembly is there for the days when the Security Council is blocked by the veto.

voices.who: Valerian Zorin (Soviet permanent representative, president of the Security Council)
voices.text: The Soviet Union has accepted the Secretary-General’s appeal. Now it is for the Secretary-General to ask the Council which article of the Charter allows a blockade on the high seas. Mediation that sidesteps legality is not mediation but acquiescence.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary)
voices.text: Go to the General Assembly, and you win the vote and lose the United States. If the United States gives up on the UN, the Cuban question will be settled outside the UN. Bombing or bargain, the Secretary-General will not be in that room.

choices.text: Join the 50 non-aligned countries in convening an emergency special session of the General Assembly, seek a resolution backing the two-to-three-week freeze, and publicly demand an answer from the United States
choices.why: When world opinion gathers on one side, even a great power backs down
choices.after: The Assembly met on the night of the 27th, and the resolution passed with 71 votes in favor. The United States and the West voted against. That same day word came that a U-2 had been shot down over Cuba. On the morning of the 28th Kennedy said only that he would “study” the Assembly resolution.

choices.text: Send the American four points you refused yesterday, now in the Secretary-General’s own words. If the Soviet ships stay outside the interception line, the freeze can survive too
choices.why: A day late, but stopping the ships at sea comes first
choices.after: Khrushchev replied that night that he had ordered the masters to wait outside the interception area. The cable was a day late, but the sea stopped. Stevenson began telephoning again, and Riad remarked quietly that the Secretary-General had sent Washington’s plan after all.

choices.text: Do as Zorin demands: reconvene the Security Council and put the Charter basis of a blockade on the high seas formally on the agenda. Mediation that sidesteps legality is acquiescence
choices.why: The Secretary-General’s first duty is to uphold the Charter
choices.after: Stevenson said in the chamber that the Secretary-General had “put the aggressor and the victim on the same scales,” and from then on the U.S. Mission to the UN began meeting the Soviet mission directly, bypassing the Secretary-General’s office. On the 27th a U-2 was shot down over Cuba.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact, at 2:26 p.m. on 25 October U Thant sent, in his own name, the second appeal the Americans wanted, and Khrushchev accepted it on the 26th. A non-aligned call for the General Assembly and Zorin’s demand on legality were both actually raised at the time, but neither was acted on.

UT-H1.unknown: At that hour reconnaissance photographs reaching Washington showed work at the bases in Cuba going on through the night. On the 27th ExComm argued into the night in Washington over Khrushchev’s letter offering the Turkish trade.

UT-H2.title: Two Weeks in New York
UT-H2.clock: About 12 days until the end of the freeze (two to three weeks)
UT-H2.event: On the 27th Khrushchev publicly proposed trading the missiles in Cuba for those in Turkey, and that same day a U-2 was shot down over Cuba. On the night of the 27th Kennedy answered Khrushchev’s letter of the 26th (withdrawal in return for a no-invasion pledge), setting as conditions a halt to work inside Cuba and verification during a freeze under UN auspices. On the 28th Khrushchev announced by radio that since he had accepted the UN freeze he would stop the work as well, but he said nothing about withdrawal. In New York today, Kuznetsov and Stevenson sit down face to face for the first time, in the Secretary-General’s office. The United States has not lifted the blockade, the Soviet ships are standing outside the interception line, and the 42 missiles are still in Cuba.
UT-H2.scene: The freeze has come about. But it has put off the war, not ended it. Two paths lie on your desk. One is to bring about, within the two or three weeks of the freeze and inside the UN framework, an agreement trading the removal of the missiles for a guarantee against invasion; the Soviets want Turkey on the table too, and the Americans refuse. The other is to secure the lifting of the blockade first and leave the missiles for later; the Soviets and Cubans want this, and the Americans will never accept it. Stevenson says that if the freeze drags on, the case for bombing will revive in Washington. Kuznetsov repeats Khrushchev’s words that if the blockade is not lifted, the order holding the ships in place is “purely temporary.” There is a rumor that London is floating the idea of placing Cuba under an international guarantee, like Belgium. You have two weeks, and every day of those two weeks someone is taking photographs.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative)
voices.text: Secretary-General, the freeze is two weeks. If the missiles are still there in two weeks, the United States loses its grounds both for keeping the blockade and for holding off an air strike. A date for removal has to come out of these two weeks.

voices.who: Vasily Kuznetsov (Soviet first deputy foreign minister)
voices.text: The Soviet Union has accepted both of the Secretary-General’s appeals. The United States has carried out neither. To talk of removal before the blockade is lifted is to put things in the wrong order.

voices.who: Word from the British side (unconfirmed rumor, gist)
voices.text: They say London is thinking of placing Cuba under an international guarantee, like Belgium, and having U Thant lead a team himself to make sure the missiles are kept inoperable while a conference goes on.

choices.text: Within the freeze, negotiate a trade of missile removal for a guarantee against invasion inside the UN framework. Keep Turkey off the agenda, and let a UN team handle verification
choices.why: Seating both sides at one document while the UN holds the framework is mediation brought to completion
choices.after: The negotiations ran past two weeks. The Soviets wanted a date first, the Americans verification first, the Cubans the lifting of the blockade first. In mid-November the Americans and Soviets agreed on a removal timetable in the Secretary-General’s office, but the missiles stayed in Cuba until December; meanwhile the Americans took photographs every day, and every day the Soviets protested.

choices.text: Secure the lifting of the blockade first. As long as the Soviet ships stay put, there is no reason to keep the blockade, and the missiles are a matter for the next stage
choices.why: End the standoff at sea first; then the problem on land can be discussed
choices.after: The United States did not lift the blockade, the Soviet Union turned its ships back, and the missiles stayed in Cuba. The freeze became a deadlock, and all through November no one moved first. The UN’s two weeks became a season.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Ending E (UN mediation) is an alternate ending in the design, showing what might have happened had the two-to-three-week freeze of the 24 October appeal actually been accepted. In fact Khrushchev announced the withdrawal on 28 October, and the freeze was never used.

UT-H2.unknown: At that hour in London, Macmillan had been talking to Kennedy on the telephone since the 25th about placing Cuba under an international guarantee, like Belgium; in their call of the 26th he raised the idea of U Thant leading a team himself to make sure the missiles were kept inoperable while a conference went on (Bundy memo).

UT-H3.title: Cordier’s Paper

telegram.from: Secretary of State Dean Rusk to Andrew Cordier (Columbia University)
telegram.to: To be passed to the Acting Secretary-General
telegram.subject: Statement in the name of the Acting Secretary-General (draft)
telegram.text: The Acting Secretary-General proposes the following for a peaceful settlement of the present crisis. / The Soviet Union will remove its missiles and their bases in Cuba under United Nations supervision. / The United States will remove its Jupiter missiles in Turkey under the same United Nations supervision. / During the removal both countries will refrain from any military action against each other’s territory and against the countries concerned.

UT-H3.event: This morning Radio Moscow made a public offer to trade the missiles in Cuba for those in Turkey, and in the afternoon word came that an American reconnaissance plane had been shot down over Cuba. Late tonight the White House released the President’s reply to Khrushchev, and it says nothing about Turkey. Since then there has been no word to the Secretary-General from Washington or Moscow. After 10 p.m. Andrew Cordier of Columbia University telephoned to say he had to see you tonight.
UT-H3.scene: At 10:30 p.m. Cordier comes into your office. You know him. He served as an under-secretary under Hammarskjöld and is said to know the workings of the Secretariat inside out. The paper he takes out holds the statement Rusk dictated: a proposal by the Acting Secretary-General that the missiles in Cuba and the Jupiters in Turkey be removed at the same time under UN supervision. Cordier says the “signal” has come. If you issue this statement, Kennedy can tell his NATO allies that “the UN proposed it,” and Khrushchev can say his public letter has been accepted. In return, Turkey will remember that the UN Secretary-General bargained away its defense, and the non-aligned will learn that the Secretary-General read out an American statement. On your desk lies Castro’s invitation, still unanswered.

voices.who: Andrew Cordier (relaying Secretary Rusk’s call, gist)
voices.text: The President will not let the Jupiters in Turkey become an obstacle to removing the missile sites in Cuba. The Jupiters are coming out in any event. Secretary Rusk telephoned me this evening on the President’s instructions and dictated a statement for you to make, proposing the removal of both the Jupiters and the missiles in Cuba. I was to put it in your hands only after a further signal from them.

voices.who: Andrew Cordier (Columbia University, former under-secretary)
voices.text: Secretary-General, the Americans wrote this, but they cannot issue it. Only the Secretary-General can. Whatever Moscow does tomorrow morning, if this paper exists tonight, both men will have room to step back.

voices.who: Ralph Bunche (under-secretary)
voices.text: Ankara will remember that the Secretary-General traded away Turkey’s defense, and the non-aligned will soon learn that the Secretary-General read out Washington’s sentences. The two powers buy face, and the UN pays the bill.

choices.text: Do not issue the statement. Hand the paper back to Cordier, and write a letter accepting Castro’s invitation
choices.why: Covering the two powers’ bargain with the UN’s name is not mediation
choices.after: Cordier folded the paper, put it away and left without a word. The document never surfaced anywhere afterward. You took out your draft letter to Havana again. Morning in Moscow was drawing near.

choices.text: Issue the statement at 11 p.m. as the Acting Secretary-General’s proposal: simultaneous removal of the missiles in Cuba and Turkey, UN supervision, and no military action during the removal
choices.why: Putting into words a deal both men have already floated is what a third party is for
choices.after: The statement went out to the wire services at 11 p.m. Moscow said in its morning broadcast that it “welcomes the proposal of the UN Secretary-General,” and Washington said it would “study” it. Ankara summoned the American ambassador that afternoon. The NATO Council met on Monday.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Rusk did dictate a statement to Cordier and have it held, but the signal was never sent and U Thant never knew. The statement itself has never been released; the wording here puts into form what Rusk’s 1987 letter describes (simultaneous removal of the Jupiters and the missiles in Cuba). Ending D (public trade) is a semi-hypothetical ending in the design.
note.src: FRUS XI d99; Phase 1 ending logic D

pressure.title: The Paper Cordier Received
pressure.text: Cordier ran the business of the Secretary-General’s office for many years under Hammarskjöld and left that year for Columbia University. What he has brought is a statement in the Acting Secretary-General’s name proposing that the missiles in Cuba and the Jupiters in Turkey be removed at the same time under UN supervision; by his account, Rusk dictated it over the telephone and told him to pass it to you only on a further signal. The first appeal was initiated by the non-aligned, and the four points of the second came in Stevenson’s hand, so this is not the first time Washington has tried to borrow the Secretary-General’s name. If you issue it, Turkey will remember that the UN Secretary-General bargained away its defense, and the non-aligned will learn that the Secretary-General read out an American statement; you can guess how both will move in the vote two months from now. There is no way, in this room tonight, to confirm that the “signal” Cordier speaks of really came from the President.

UT-H3.unknown: At that hour in Washington, ExComm argued for three hours from 4 p.m. over how to answer Khrushchev’s public letter (the Turkish trade), and Kennedy’s reply, sent at 8:05 p.m., accepted the private letter of the night of the 26th. Earlier, at 7:45, Robert Kennedy had met Ambassador Dobrynin. In reality the signal to deliver the statement Rusk dictated to Cordier never came, and U Thant never knew of it. The episode first came to light in Rusk’s letter of 1987.

UT-H4.title: Staying in New York
UT-H4.clock: One day until Mikoyan arrives in New York (1 November)
UT-H4.event: On the morning of the 28th Radio Moscow announced the withdrawal, and Havana announced its five conditions. On the 29th American reconnaissance planes flew over Cuba again and Cuban batteries fired on them. Kuznetsov put forward the Red Cross plan for inspecting ships, and the White House is keeping the quarantine in place “day by day.” With the Secretary-General not going to Havana, Cuba has stated no position at all on inspection, and there is not a single UN staff member inside Cuba. Tomorrow Mikoyan passes through New York on his way to Havana.
UT-H4.scene: You stayed in New York, and no one went to Cuba. To your cable offering to send Loutfi and Rikhye in your place, Havana replied only that “it was the Secretary-General who was invited.” Stevenson says that if Cuba refuses inspection, the United States will keep up reconnaissance and keep the blockade too. Kuznetsov says the Soviet Union has honored both of the Secretary-General’s appeals and the United States neither. Lechuga says quietly that Cuba can talk to the Secretary-General, but a Secretary-General arriving with an American inspection team is another matter. Since the Cuban batteries fired on American planes on the 29th, word has been going around the delegations that if they fire again, Washington will hit the SAM sites. You have two paths left: work out the form of inspection in New York with Mikoyan and Stevenson, without having sent anyone; or make the dispatch of a UN inspection team official with a Security Council resolution and present it to Cuba.

voices.who: Carlos Lechuga (Cuban permanent representative)
voices.text: Cuba invited the Secretary-General. That the Secretary-General did not come was not Cuba’s decision. Send an inspection team by Security Council document, and it will be read as an American document.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative)
voices.text: Secretary-General, Khrushchev promised UN verification. If Cuba blocks it, that is the Soviets’ problem. If the UN cannot get in, the United States will watch from the air. If Cuba fires on those planes, that will be a different story.

voices.who: Brigadier I. J. Rikhye (military adviser)
voices.text: I can gather ten Swedish, Ethiopian and Indian officers. But we cannot land at Havana airport without a cable of invitation from the Cuban government. We have the plane; we don’t have permission to land.

choices.text: Without having sent Loutfi and Rikhye, work out the form of verification in New York with Mikoyan, Kuznetsov and Stevenson. Deal with Cuba through Lechuga
choices.why: Even if you cannot get to the scene, the agreement will be written in New York
choices.after: On the evening of 1 November Mikoyan spent four hours pressing to link the five conditions to the U.S.–Soviet agreement, and the Americans replied “one issue only.” Major Anderson’s body came back from Havana only on 4 November. In the Havana the Secretary-General never visited, Mikoyan spent three weeks.

choices.text: Make the dispatch of a UN inspection team official with a Security Council resolution. Get Khrushchev’s promise of 28 October down on paper and present it to Cuba
choices.why: Establishing a Council mandate is quicker than waiting for Cuba’s consent
choices.after: Ireland and Chile tabled the draft resolution, and the Soviet Union said it would veto it unless the phrase “with the consent of Cuba” was included. Lechuga cabled Havana that evening.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact U Thant went to Havana on 30–31 October and, though he did not get inspection, obtained the return of Major Anderson’s body and confirmation that the dismantling was under way. The Cuban fire of the 29th is recorded in a State Department cable: “today one reconnaissance plane drew fire from Cuban forces.”

UT-H4.unknown: At that hour in Washington, after the Cuban batteries fired on an American reconnaissance plane on the 29th, talk of reprisals against the SAM sites had revived. A State Department cable records: “today one reconnaissance plane drew fire from Cuban forces.”

UT-H5.place: UN Headquarters, the Secretary-General’s anteroom beside the Security Council chamber
UT-H5.title: A Plane Without Permission to Land
UT-H5.clock: One day until the Security Council vote

telegram.from: Fidel Castro, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba (through Permanent Representative Lechuga)
telegram.to: U Thant, Acting Secretary-General of the United Nations
telegram.subject: Rejection of unilateral inspection, and violations of Cuban airspace
telegram.text: As Cuba has informed you and has publicly reiterated, it does not accept unilateral inspection of Cuban territory by any body, national or international. / Our airspace and our sovereignty will never be a matter for negotiation. / Any warplane that enters Cuban airspace and violates our sovereignty must run the risk of being shot down within range of our anti-aircraft weapons.

UT-H5.event: Rikhye has drawn up a list of 12 Swedish, Ethiopian, Indian and Brazilian officers for a verification team, and a chartered Varig plane is standing by at Idlewild. Before the Security Council is a draft resolution asking the Secretary-General to send a verification team, and the Soviet Union has said it will veto it unless the phrase “with the consent of the Cuban government” is added. Castro’s letter came yesterday, and American low-level reconnaissance resumed today. In Havana Mikoyan has spent two weeks trying to persuade Castro, and all 42 missiles have gone out to sea. No one can say whether Cuba will order anti-aircraft fire again.
UT-H5.scene: The verification team exists; the permission to land does not. If you force a vote, the Soviet Union will veto, and the record will show that the Soviet Union itself blocked the “verification by UN representatives” Khrushchev promised on 28 October. The Americans say that would be enough for them. Kuznetsov says that if that record is made, the Soviet Union will cut the UN out of the bilateral U.S.–Soviet talks. Lechuga says Cuba can still talk to the Secretary-General, but if the resolution passes, that door will close too. The U.S. Navy has already counted the 42 departing missiles at sea; what remains is the Il-28 bombers and a date for lifting the blockade, and the Americans and Soviets are settling that between themselves. You must decide whether to go to a vote for the sake of the UN’s record, or withdraw the resolution for the sake of the UN’s place at the table.

voices.who: Fidel Castro to U Thant (letter of yesterday)
voices.text: As Cuba has informed you and has publicly reiterated, it does not accept unilateral inspection of Cuban territory by any body, national or international.

voices.who: Vasily Kuznetsov (Soviet first deputy foreign minister)
voices.text: The Soviet Union has shipped out all the missiles, and the Americans counted them at sea. If the Secretary-General puts an inspection team without Cuba’s consent to a vote, the Soviet Union will have no choice but to oppose it, and from then on we will negotiate with the Americans alone.

voices.who: Adlai Stevenson (U.S. permanent representative)
voices.text: Put it to a vote. If the Soviets veto it, the world will see who broke the promise. Inspection team or no, the United States watches from the air, and we counted them at sea.

choices.text: Withdraw the resolution. Disband the verification team, and propose to the American and Soviet missions a closing procedure in which the United States, the Soviet Union and the Secretary-General each make a declaration in the Security Council
choices.why: Keeping the UN in the room for the next crisis matters more than a single entry in the record
choices.after: On 20 November Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade, and on 7 January 1963 the United States and the Soviet Union sent the Security Council a joint letter and had the matter taken off the agenda. The Secretary-General’s declaration was cited in that letter in a single sentence. The UN never once got inside Cuba.

choices.text: Force the vote. Even if the Soviet Union vetoes it, put on the record who promised UN verification and who blocked it
choices.why: Promises are kept next time only if there is a record this time
choices.after: Seven in favor, two against (the Soviet Union and Romania), two abstentions. The Soviet veto defeated the resolution. From that night Kuznetsov and McCloy met without going through the Secretary-General’s office, and the Il-28s and the lifting of the blockade were settled in that room. On 20 November Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact U Thant never brought the dispatch of an inspection team without Cuba’s consent before the Security Council; in mid-November he explored a “mobile verification team” of neutral personnel and the formula “verification, not inspection.” After 26 November the UN was effectively shut out of the bilateral U.S.–Soviet negotiations, and on 7 January 1963 the matter was taken off the Council’s agenda by a joint U.S.–Soviet letter (S/5227).

map.caption: New York is about 2,100 kilometers from Havana.

UT-H5.unknown: In Havana the next day, 17 November, the Cuban forces authorized anti-aircraft fire, and they withdrew the order on the 18th. Soviet forces had already rendered all the missiles inoperable on 2 November, and McCloy and Kuznetsov confirmed the figures on 4 November.

epilogues.A: On 30 November 1962 the General Assembly unanimously elected U Thant secretary-general for a full term, and he served two terms, until 1971. In March 1963 Stevenson testified to the Senate that the Secretary-General’s intervention had been an “indispensable first step” toward a peaceful settlement, but what Washington and London had called his appeal on the night of 24 October came out only later. The UN never once got inside Cuba, and the missiles were counted at sea by the US Navy. At that same hour, in Kennedy’s room, ExComm was holding its last meeting on the dates for the Il-28 bombers and the lifting of the blockade.
epilogues.D: The missiles in Cuba and in Turkey were withdrawn together under UN supervision, and the world remembered it as the UN secretary-general’s proposal. Ankara did not remember it that way. The NATO Council held that the United States had bargained away the defense of an ally through the mouth of a third party, and in the vote on U Thant’s election to a full term, Turkey abstained.
epilogues.E: The two-week freeze stretched into a season. The missiles left Cuba in December, and the Americans and Soviets signed the removal timetable in the Secretary-General’s office. The UN was in that room. But in the United States people went on saying that “the UN kept the missiles in Cuba two months longer,” and in the next crisis Washington did not turn to New York first.
epilogues.F: The Soviet ships stand outside the interception line, the American warships ride on it, and the missiles are in Cuba. No one has fired, and no one has backed down. When a new crisis began in Berlin in the spring of 1963, the ships in the Caribbean were still where they had been.

dossier.t: Born on 22 January 1909 at Pantanaw in the Irrawaddy delta of Burma, you are 53 in October 1962. The eldest of four sons, you lost your father at 14, left Rangoon University after two years because of the family’s circumstances, and went home to teach at the Pantanaw National High School and later serve as its headmaster. There you became friends with U Nu, who had come to the school as superintendent. After independence you worked at Prime Minister U Nu’s side, as director of information in 1947 and director of broadcasting in 1948, and in 1957 you came to New York as Burma’s permanent representative to the UN. After Secretary-General Hammarskjöld died over the Congo in September 1961, the General Assembly chose you as acting secretary-general on 3 November, and for the thirteen months since you have led the Secretariat with the word “acting” attached to your title. You are a Buddhist who meditates every day, known as a man who never raises his voice and speaks in sentences as orderly as a document. In 1962 your son Tin Maung died in an accident in Rangoon; your wife, Daw Thein Tin, and your daughter, Aye Aye Thant, are with you.

Ralph Bunche, under-secretary for special political affairs, is an American who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1950 and ran the Congo operation under Hammarskjöld. He says that if the Secretary-General speaks on the first day, he will be read as taking one side, and he warns that unless your cable calls for a halt to construction inside Cuba, Washington will read the appeal as pro-Soviet. Under-Secretary Omar Loutfi, an Egyptian diplomat, is your channel to the Asian and African delegates outside the chamber, and he is the one who says that if the non-aligned walk away, the Secretary-General is left with nothing. Your chef de cabinet, Narasimhan, a former Indian civil servant, handles papers and schedules. Your military adviser, Brigadier Rikhye, an Indian Army officer who served in the Congo operation, is preparing neutral military technicians, aircraft and an independent communications link. Andrew Cordier, Hammarskjöld’s aide, left that year for Columbia University but is still close to Rusk. In the chamber are Stevenson of the United States; Zorin of the Soviet Union, president of the Security Council for October; García-Incháustegui and Lechuga of Cuba; and Riad of the United Arab Republic and Quaison-Sackey of Ghana.

Your first worry is your own position. Your full term hangs on a General Assembly vote two months away, and you know how the Soviet Union has regarded this office since Khrushchev demanded in 1960 that it be split three ways. Some read your silence as resting on a calculation: the moment you were seen to take sides, you would lose the votes and the post. The second is the non-aligned delegations outside the chamber. Delegates from nearly fifty countries want to put the Secretary-General out in front, and their freeze proposal leans toward the Soviet side, so the West will not accept it. The third is Article 99 of the Charter. It says only that the secretary-general may bring to the attention of the Security Council a matter that threatens the peace. Hammarskjöld invoked it in 1960 to bring the Congo before the Council, and thirteen months ago he did not come back from the Congo. Your hope is a freeze of two to three weeks that gives the two leaders time to meet, with the UN inside that room rather than outside it.

movers.intro: Whether U Thant’s appeals halted the crisis, or merely lent the UN’s name to a course the two great powers had already chosen, has long divided opinion. The main views are these:
views: Walter Dorn and Robert Pauk: in a 2009 article they call U Thant an “unsung mediator,” arguing that his first appeal of 24 October opened a way for Khrushchev to back down without losing face, that his second appeal of 25 October prevented a clash at sea, and that his trip to Havana filled the gap left after the settlement. They hold that the fact that the United States drafted the second appeal does not diminish its effect.

Ramses Nassif: U Thant’s press officer at the time, he recalls that U Thant played down his own role and that his Buddhist equanimity was the basis of the trust he won between the two great powers. He cites as evidence Stevenson’s testimony to the Senate in 1963 that the Secretary-General’s intervention had been an indispensable first step toward a peaceful settlement.

Bernard Firestone: covering U Thant’s whole tenure, he argues that the Cuban crisis established his standing before his election to a full term, but that Washington and Moscow settled the terms of the agreement between themselves, and the UN’s role was to open the way and buy time.

Michael Dobbs: following the Washington record, he finds that Kennedy’s aides at first did not welcome the appeal of 24 October, but Kennedy himself saw at once that it offered Khrushchev a way out. He explains that U Thant’s value lay less in the substance of his proposals than in a third party’s name, which let the two leaders stop without conceding anything to each other directly.
movers.note: The UN’s only record of U Thant’s talks in Havana is its press releases, and the details rest on the transcript Cuba made public and on Rikhye’s memoirs. What you won in that room, and how much, therefore reads differently depending on whose record you read.
